entries.8a6aa3727b99ac3fa70d6c130a02703885a49e0e: <div sID="gen32163" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="1Thess.2" sID="1Thess.2"/> <div eID="gen32163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32164" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32165" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle puts the Thessalonians in mind of the manner of his preaching among them, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.1-1Thess.2.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. Then of the manner of his conversation among them, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.7-1Thess.2.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. Afterwards of the success of his ministry, with the effects both on himself and on them (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13-1Thess.2.16">ver. 13-16</reference>), and then apologizes for his absence, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17-1Thess.2.20">ver. 17-20</reference>.
entries.78fe3720ad1852b03b06f96d4b24e44b88c7f4bd: <div eID="gen32165" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32164" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Primitive Ministers. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32166" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For yourselves, brethren, know our entrance in unto you, that it was not in vain: <hi type="super">2</hi> But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention. <hi type="super">3</hi> For our exhortation <hi type="italic">was</hi> not of deceit, nor of uncleanness, nor in guile: <hi type="super">4</hi> But as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts. 5 For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloak of covetousness; God <hi type="italic">is</hi> witness: <hi type="super">6</hi> Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor <hi type="italic">yet</hi> of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ. <div eID="gen32166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32167" type="x-p"/> Here we have an account of Paul's manner of preaching, and his comfortable reflection upon his entrance in among the Thessalonians. As he had the testimony of his own conscience witnessing to his integrity, so he could appeal to the Thessalonians how faithful he, and Silas, and Timotheus, his helpers in the work of the Lord, had discharged their office: <hi type="italic">You yourselves, brethren, know our entrance in unto you.</hi> Note, It is a great comfort to a minister to have his own conscience and the consciences of others witnessing for him that he set out well, with good designs and from good principles; and that <hi type="italic">his preaching was not in vain,</hi> or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">was not fain.</hi> The apostle here comforts himself either in the success of his ministry, that it was not fruitless or in vain (according to our translation), or as others think, reflecting upon the sincerity of his preaching, that it was not vain and empty, or deceitful and treacherous. The subject-matter of the apostle's preaching was not vain and idle speculations about useless niceties and foolish questions, but sound and solid truth, such as was most likely to profit his hearers. A good example this is, to be imitated by all the ministers of the gospel. Much less was the apostle's preaching vain or deceitful. He could say to these Thessalonians what he told the Corinthians (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2 Cor. iv. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully.</hi> He had no sinister or worldly design in his preaching, which he puts them in mind to have been, <div eID="gen32167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32168" type="x-p"/> I. With courage and resolution: <hi type="italic">We were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">v. 2</reference>. The apostle was inspired with a holy boldness, nor was he discouraged at the afflictions he met with, or the opposition that was made against him. He had met with ill usage at Philippi, as these Thessalonians well knew. There it was that he and Silas were shamefully treated, being put in the stocks; yet no sooner were they set at liberty than they went to Thessalonica, and preached the gospel with as much boldness as ever. Note, Suffering in a good cause should rather sharpen than blunt the edge of holy resolution. The gospel of Christ, at its first setting out in the world, met with much opposition; and those who preached it preached it <hi type="italic">with contention,</hi> with great agony, which denoted either the apostles' striving in their preaching or their striving against the opposition they met with. This was Paul's comfort; he was neither daunted in his work, nor driven from it. <div eID="gen32168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32169" type="x-p"/> II. With great simplicity and godly sincerity: <hi type="italic">Our exhortation was not of deceit, nor of uncleanness, nor in guile,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.3">v. 3</reference>. This, no doubt, was matter of the greatest comfort to the apostle—the consciousness of his own sincerity; and was one reason of his success. It was the sincere and uncorrupted gospel that he preached and exhorted them to believe and obey. His design was not to set up a faction, to draw men over to a party, but to promote <hi type="italic">pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father.</hi> The gospel he preached was without deceit, it was true and faithful; it was not fallacious, nor a cunningly-devised fable. Nor was it of uncleanness. His gospel was pure and holy, worthy of its holy author, tending to discountenance all manner of impurity. <hi type="italic">The word of God is pure.</hi> There should be no corrupt mixtures therewith; and, as the matter of the apostle's exhortation was thus true and pure, the manner of his speaking was without guile. He did not pretend one thing and intend another. <hi type="italic">He believed, and therefore he spoke.</hi> He had no sinister and secular aims and views, but was in reality what he seemed to be. The apostle not only asserts his sincerity, but subjoins the reasons and evidences thereof. The reasons are contained, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.4">v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen32169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32170" type="x-p"/> 1. They were stewards, <hi type="italic">put in trust</hi> with the gospel: and it is required of a steward that he be faithful. The gospel which Paul preached was not his own, but the gospel of God. Note, Ministers have a great favour shown them, and honour put upon them, and trust committed to them. They must not dare to corrupt the word of God: they must diligently make use of what is entrusted with them, so as God hath allowed and commanded, knowing they shall be called to an account, when they must be no longer stewards. <div eID="gen32170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32171" type="x-p"/> 2. Their design was to please God and not men. God is a God of truth, and requires truth in the inward parts; and, if sincerity be wanting, all that we do cannot please God. The gospel of Christ is not accommodated to the fain fancies and lusts of men, to gratify their appetites and passions; but, on the contrary, it was designed for the mortifying of their corrupt affections, and delivering them from the power of fancy, that they might be brought under the power of faith. <hi type="italic">If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Gal. i. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen32171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32172" type="x-p"/> 3. They acted under the consideration of God's omniscience, as in the sight of him who <hi type="italic">tries our hearts.</hi> This is indeed the great motive to sincerity, to consider that God not only seeth all that we do, but knoweth our thoughts afar off, and searcheth the heart. He is well acquainted with all our aims and designs, as well as our actions. And it is from this God who trieth our hearts that we must receive our reward. The evidences of the apostle's sincerity follow; and they are these:—(1.) He avoided flattery: <hi type="italic">Neither at any time used we flattering words, as you know,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">v. 5</reference>. He and his fellow-labourers preached Christ and him crucified, and did not aim to gain an interest in men's affections for themselves, by glorying, and fawning and wheedling them. No, he was far from this; nor did he flatter men in their sins; nor tell them, if they would be of his party, they might live as they listed. He did not flatter them with fain hopes, nor indulge them in any evil work or way, promising them life, and so <hi type="italic">daubing with untempered mortar.</hi> (2.) He avoided covetousness. He did not make the ministry <hi type="italic">a cloak,</hi> or a covering, for <hi type="italic">covetousness, as God was witness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">v. 5</reference>. His design was not to enrich himself by preaching the gospel; so far from this, he did not stipulate with them for bread. He was not like the false apostles, who, <hi type="italic">through covetousness, with feigned words made merchandise</hi> of the people, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.3">2 Pet. ii. 3</reference>. (3.) He avoided ambition and vain-glory: <hi type="italic">Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you nor yet of others,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.6">v. 6</reference>. They expected neither people's purses nor their caps, neither to be enriched by them nor caressed, and adored, and called Rabbi by them. This apostle exhorts the Galatians (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.26">ch. v. 26</reference>) <hi type="italic">not to be desirous of vain glory;</hi> his ambition was to obtain <hi type="italic">that honour which comes from God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.44">John v. 44</reference>. He tells them that they might have used greater authority as apostles, and expected greater esteem, and demanded maintenance, which is meant by the phrase of <hi type="italic">being burdensome,</hi> because perhaps some would have thought this too great a burden for them to bear.
entries.7e9cceec5a95e4b7228f2ec5ba4fbdbc6b89280a: <div eID="gen32172" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Primitive Ministers. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children: <hi type="super">8</hi> So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us. 9 For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God. <hi type="super">10</hi> Ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> witnesses, and God <hi type="italic">also,</hi> how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe: <hi type="super">11</hi> As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father <hi type="italic">doth</hi> his children, <hi type="super">12</hi> That ye would walk worthy of God, who hath called you unto his kingdom and glory. <div eID="gen32173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32174" type="x-p"/> In these words the apostle reminds the Thessalonians of the manner of his conversation among them. And, <div eID="gen32174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32175" type="x-p"/> I. He mentions the gentleness of their behaviour: <hi type="italic">We were gentle among you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.7">v. 7</reference>. He showed great mildness and tenderness who might have acted with the authority of an apostle of Christ. Such behaviour greatly recommends religion, and is most agreeable to God's gracious dealing with sinners, in and by the gospel. This great apostle, though he abhorred and avoided flattery, was most condescending to all men. He accommodated himself to all men's capacities, <hi type="italic">and became all things to all men.</hi> He showed the kindness and care of a nurse that cherishes her children. This is the way to win people, rather than to rule with rigour. The word of God is indeed powerful; and as it comes often with awful authority upon the minds of men, as it always has enough in it to convince every impartial judgment, so it comes with the more pleasing power, when the ministers of the gospel recommend themselves to the affections of the people. And as a nursing mother bears with frowardness in a child, and condescends to mean offices for its good, and draws out her breast, cherishing it in her bosom, so in like manner should the ministers of Christ behave towards their people. The <hi type="italic">servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, and patient,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2 Tim. ii. 24</reference>. This gentleness and goodness the apostle expressed several ways. 1. By the most affectionate desire of their welfare: <hi type="italic">Being affectionately desirous of you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.8">v. 8</reference>. The apostle had a most affectionate love to their persons, and sought them, not theirs; themselves, not their goods; and to gain them, not to be a gainer by them, or to make a merchandise of them: it was their spiritual and eternal welfare and salvation that he was earnestly desirous of. 2. By great readiness to do them good, willingly imparting to them, <hi type="italic">not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.8">v. 8</reference>. See here the manner of Paul's preaching. He spared no pains therein. He was willing to run hazards, and venture his soul, or life, in preaching the gospel. He was willing to spend and be spent in the service of men's souls; and, as those who give bread to the hungry from a charitable principle are said to impart their souls in what they give (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.10">Isa. xviii. 10</reference>), so did the apostles in giving forth the bread of life; so dear were these Thessalonians in particular to this apostle, and so great was his love to them. 3. By bodily labour to prevent their charge, or that his ministry might not be expensive and burdensome to them: <hi type="italic">You remember our labour and travail; for, labouring night and day,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">v. 9</reference>. He denied himself the liberty he had of taking wages from the churches. To the labour of the ministry he added that of his calling, as a tent-maker, that he might get his own bread. We are not to suppose that the apostle spent the whole night and day in bodily labour, or work, to supply the necessities of his body; for then he would have had no time for the work of the ministry. But he spent part of the night, as well as the day, in this work; and was willing to forego his rest in the night, that he might have an opportunity to do good to the souls of men in the day time. A good example is here set before the ministers of the gospel, to be industrious for the salvation of men's souls, though it will not follow that they are always obliged to preach freely. There is no general rule to be drawn from this instance, either that ministers may at no time work with their hands, for the supply of their outward necessities, or that they ought always to do so. 4. By the holiness of their conversation, concerning which he appeals not only to them, but to God also (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">You are witnesses, and God also.</hi> They were observers of their outward conversation in public before men, and God was witness not only of their behaviour in secret, but of the inward principles from which they acted. Their behaviour was holy towards God, just towards all men, and unblamable, without giving cause of scandal or offence; and they were careful to give no offence either to those who were without, or to those who believed, that they might give no ill example; that their preaching and living might be all of a piece. Herein, said this apostle, <hi type="italic">do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence towards God, and towards men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Acts xxiv. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen32175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32176" type="x-p"/> II. He mentions their faithful discharge of the work and office of the ministry, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.11-1Thess.2.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Concerning this also he could appeal to them as witnesses. Paul and his fellow-labourers were not only good Christians, but faithful ministers. And we should not only be good as to our general calling as Christians, but in our particular callings and relations. Paul exhorted the Thessalonians, not only informing them in their duty, but exciting and quickening them to the performance of it, by proper motives and arguments. And he comforted them also, endeavouring to cheer and support their spirits under the difficulties and discouragements they might meet with. And this he did not only publicly, but privately also, and from house to house (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.20">Acts xx. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">and charged every one</hi> of them by personal addresses: this, some think, is intended by the similitude of a father's charging his children. This expression also denotes the affectionate and compassionate counsels and consolations which this apostle used. He was their spiritual father; and, as he cherished them like a nursing mother, so he charged them as a father, with a father's affection rather than a father's authority. As <hi type="italic">my beloved sons, I warn you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">1 Cor. iv. 14</reference>. The manner of this apostle's exhortation ought to be regarded by ministers in particular for their imitation, and the matter of it is greatly to be regarded by them and all others; namely, that <hi type="italic">they would walk worthy of God, who hath called them to his kingdom and glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.12">v. 12</reference>. Observe, 1. What is our great gospel privilege—that God has called us to his kingdom and glory. The gospel calls us into the kingdom and state of grace here and unto the kingdom and state of glory hereafter, to heaven and happiness as our end and to holiness as the way to that end. 2. What is our great gospel duty—that we walk worthy of God, that the temper of our minds and tenour of our lives be answerable to this call and suitable to this privilege. We should accommodate ourselves to the intention and design of the gospel, and live suitably to our profession and privileges, our hopes and expectations, as becomes those who are called with such a high and holy calling.
entries.ab0cb3a346f63e64d2e7e2bbde710e0ab67d0ba2: <div eID="gen32176" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Effects of the Christian Ministry. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32177" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received <hi type="italic">it</hi> not <hi type="italic">as</hi> the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe. <hi type="super">14</hi> For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judæa are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they <hi type="italic">have</hi> of the Jews: <hi type="super">15</hi> Who both killed the Lord Jesus, and their own prophets, and have persecuted us; and they please not God, and are contrary to all men: <hi type="super">16</hi> Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved, to fill up their sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost. <div eID="gen32177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32178" type="x-p"/> Here observe, I. The apostle makes mention of the success of his ministry among these Thessalonians (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">v. 13</reference>), which is expressed, <div eID="gen32178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32179" type="x-p"/> 1. By the manner of their receiving the word of God: <hi type="italic">When you received the word of God, which you heard of us, you received it, not as the word of men, but (as it is in truth) the word of God.</hi> Where note, (1.) The word of the gospel is preached by men like ourselves, men of like passions and infirmities with others: <hi type="italic">We have this treasure in earthen vessels.</hi> The word of God, which these Thessalonians received, they heard from the apostles. (2.) However, it is in truth the word of God. Such was the word the apostles preached by divine inspiration, and such is that which is left upon record, written in the scriptures by divine inspiration; and such is that word which in our days is preached, being either contained, or evidently founded on, or deduced from, these sacred oracles. (3.) Those are greatly to blame who give out their own fancies or injunctions for the word of God. This is the vilest way of imposing upon a people, and to deal unfaithfully. (4.) Those are also to blame who, in hearing the word, look no further than to the ministry of men, who are only, or chiefly, pleased with the elegance of the style, or the beauty of the composition, or the voice and manner in which the word is preached, and expect to receive their advantage herein. (5.) We should receive the word of God as the word of God, with affections suitable to the holiness, wisdom, verity, and goodness, thereof. The words of men are frail and perishing, like themselves, and sometimes false, foolish, and fickle: but God's word is holy, wise, just, and faithful; and, like its author, lives and abides for ever. Let us accordingly receive and regard it. <div eID="gen32179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32180" type="x-p"/> 2. By the wonderful operation of this word they received: <hi type="italic">It effectually worketh in those that believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">v. 13</reference>. Those who by faith receive the word find it profitable. <hi type="italic">It does good to those that walk uprightly,</hi> and by its wonderful effects evidences itself to be the word of God. This converts their souls, and enlightens their minds, and rejoices their hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Ps. xix.</reference>); and such as have this inward testimony of the truth of the scriptures, the word of God, by the effectual operations thereof on their hearts, have the best evidence of their divine original to themselves, though this is not sufficient to convince others who are strangers thereto. <div eID="gen32180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32181" type="x-p"/> II. He mentions the good effects which his successful preaching had, <div eID="gen32181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32182" type="x-p"/> 1. Upon himself and fellow-labourers. It was a constant cause of thankfulness: <hi type="italic">For this cause thank we God without ceasing,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">v. 13</reference>. The apostle expressed his thankfulness to God so often upon this account that he seemed to think he never could be sufficiently thankful that God had counted him faithful, and put him into the ministry, and made his ministrations successful. <div eID="gen32182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32183" type="x-p"/> 2. Upon them. The word wrought effectually in them, not only to be examples unto others in faith and good works (which he had mentioned before), but also in constancy and patience under sufferings and trials for the sake of the gospel: <hi type="italic">You became followers of the churches of God, and have suffered like things as they have done</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.14">v. 14</reference>), and with like courage and constancy, with like patience and hope. Note, The cross is the Christian's mark: if we are called to suffer we are called only to be followers of the churches of God; <hi type="italic">so persecuted they the prophets that were before you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">Matt. v. 12</reference>. It is a good effect of the gospel when we are enabled to suffer for its sake. The apostle mentions the sufferings of the churches of God, which <hi type="italic">in Judea were in Christ Jesus.</hi> Those in Judea first heard the gospel, and they first suffered for it: for the Jews were the most bitter enemies Christianity had, and were especially enraged against their countrymen who embraced Christianity. Note, Bitter zeal and fiery persecution will set countrymen at variance, and break through all the bonds of nature, as well as contradict all the rules of religion. In every city where the apostles went to preach the gospel the Jews stirred up the inhabitants against them. They were the ringleaders of persecution in all places; so in particular it was at Thessalonica: <reference osisRef="Acts.17.5">Acts xvii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Jews that believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city in an uproar.</hi> Upon this occasion, the apostle gives a character of the unbelieving Jews (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">v. 15</reference>), enough to justify their final rejection and the ruin of their place, and church, and nation, which was now approaching. (1.) They <hi type="italic">killed the Lord Jesus,</hi> and impudently and presumptuously wished that his blood might be on them and their children. (2.) They killed <hi type="italic">their own prophets:</hi> so they had done all along; their fathers had done so: they had been a persecuting generation. (3.) They hated the apostles, and did them all the mischief they could. They persecuted them, and drove and chased them from place to place: and no marvel, if they killed the Lord Jesus, that they persecuted his followers. (4.) They <hi type="italic">pleased not God.</hi> They had quite lost all sense of religion, and due care to do their duty to God. It was a most fatal mistake to think that they did God service by killing God's servants. Murder and persecution are most hateful to God and cannot be justified on any pretence; they are so contrary to natural religion that no zeal for any true or only pretended institution of religion can ever excuse them. (5.) They were <hi type="italic">contrary to all men.</hi> Their persecuting spirit was a perverse spirit; contrary to the light of nature, and contrary to humanity, contrary to the welfare of all men, and contrary to the sentiments of all men not under the power of bigotry. (6.) They had <hi type="italic">an implacable enmity to the Gentiles,</hi> and envied them the offers of the gospel: <hi type="italic">Forbidding the apostles to speak to the Gentiles, that they might be saved.</hi> The means of salvation had long been confined to the Jews. <hi type="italic">Salvation is of the Jews,</hi> says our Saviour. And they were envious against the Gentiles, and angry that they should be admitted to share in the means of salvation. Nothing provoked them more than our Saviour's speaking to them at any time concerning this matter; this enraged the Jews at Jerusalem, when, in his defence, Paul told them, <hi type="italic">he was sent unto the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.22.21">Acts xxii. 21</reference>. They heard him patiently till he uttered these words, but then could endure no longer, but <hi type="italic">lifted up their voices, and said, Away with such a fellow from the earth, for it is not fit that he should live.</hi> Thus did the Jews fill up their sins; and nothing tends more to any person or people's filling up the measure of their sins than opposing the gospel, obstructing the progress of it, and hindering the salvation of precious souls. For the sake of these things <hi type="italic">wrath has come upon them to the uttermost;</hi> that is, wrath was determined against them, and would soon overtake them. It was not many years after this that Jerusalem was destroyed, and the Jewish nation cut off by the Romans. Note, When the measure of any man's iniquity is full, and he has sinned to the uttermost, then comes wrath, and that to the uttermost.
entries.e7129984308528976a94abe3bf841daee48c8ef4: <div eID="gen32183" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Effects of the Christian Ministry. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32184" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire. <hi type="super">18</hi> Wherefore we would have come unto you, even I Paul, once and again; but Satan hindered us. <hi type="super">19</hi> For what <hi type="italic">is</hi> our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? <hi type="italic">Are</hi> not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? <hi type="super">20</hi> For ye are our glory and joy. <div eID="gen32184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32185" type="x-p"/> In these words the apostle apologizes for his absence. Here observe, 1. He tells them they were involuntarily forced from them: <hi type="italic">We, brethren, were taken from you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17">v. 17</reference>. Such was the rage of his persecutors. He was unwillingly sent away by night to Berea, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.10">Acts xvii. 10</reference>. 2. Though he was absent in body, yet he was present in heart. He had still a remembrance of them, and great care for them. 3. Even his bodily absence was but for a short time, the time of an hour. Time is short, all our time on earth is short and uncertain, whether we are present with our friends or absent from them. This world is not a place where we are always, or long, to be together. It is in heaven that holy souls shall meet, and never part more. 4. He earnestly desired and endeavoured to see them again: <hi type="italic">We endeavoured more abundantly to see your face with great desire,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17">v. 17</reference>. So that the apostle at least intended his absence should be but for a short time. His desire and endeavour were to return again very soon to Thessalonica. But men of business are not masters of their own time. Paul did his endeavour, and he could do no more, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.18">v. 18</reference>. 5. He tells them that Satan hindered his return (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.18">v. 18</reference>), that is, either some enemy or enemies, or the great enemy of mankind, who stirred up opposition to Paul, either in his return to Thessalonica, when he intended to return thither, or stirred up such contentions or dissensions in those places whether he went as made his presence necessary. Note, Satan is a constant enemy to the work of God, and does all he can to obstruct it. 6. He assures them of his affection and high esteem for them, though he was not able, as yet, to be present with them according to his desire. They were his <hi type="italic">hope, and joy, and crown of rejoicing; his glory and joy.</hi> These are expressions of great and endeared affection, and high estimation. And it is happy when ministers and people have such mutual affection and esteem of each other, and especially if they shall thus rejoice, if those that sow and those that reap shall rejoice together, <hi type="italic">in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming.</hi> <div eID="gen32185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32186" type="x-p"/> The apostle here puts the Thessalonians in mind that though he could not come to them as yet, and though he should never be able to come to them, yet our Lord Jesus Christ will come, nothing shall hinder this. And further, when he shall come, all must appear in his presence, or before him. Ministers and people must all appear before him, and faithful people will be the glory and joy of faithful ministers in that great and glorious day.  <chapter eID="1Thess.2"/> <div eID="gen32186" type="x-p"/>

entries.e1c42f8b29cb29f744858de17969b119d3a26128: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17930"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen36619" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.1-1Thess.2.20">1Th 2:1-20</reference>. His Manner of Preaching, and Theirs of Receiving, the Gospel; His Desire to Have Revisited Them Frustrated by Satan.<div eID="gen36619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17930"/><hi type="bold">1. For--</hi>confirming <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference>. He discusses the manner of his fellow missionaries' preaching among them (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>, and former part of <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>) at <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.1-1Thess.2.12">1Th 2:1-12</reference>; and the Thessalonians' reception of the word (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">1Th 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>, and latter part of <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>) at <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13-1Thess.2.16">1Th 2:13-16</reference>.<div eID="gen36620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yourselves--</hi>Not only do strangers report it, but you know it to be true [Alford] "yourselves."<div eID="gen36621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not in vain--</hi>Greek, "not vain," that is, it was full of "power" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>). The Greek for "was," expresses rather "hath been and is," implying the permanent and continuing character of his preaching. <div eID="gen36622" type="x-p"/>
entries.55231c88ebd4b034c3978edc93964ca90c356f15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17931"/><div sID="gen36623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17931"/><hi type="bold">2. even after that we had suffered before--</hi>at Philippi (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.11-Acts.16.40">Ac 16:11-40</reference>): a circumstance which would have deterred mere natural, unspiritual men from further preaching.<div eID="gen36623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shamefully entreated--</hi>ignominiously scourged (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.22">Ac 16:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen36624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bold--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.4.29">Ac 4:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">Ep 6:20</reference>).<div eID="gen36625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in our God--</hi>The ground of our boldness in speaking was the realization of God as "OUR God."<div eID="gen36626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with much contention--</hi>that is, literally, as of competitors in a contest: striving earnestness (<reference osisRef="Col.1.29">Col 1:29</reference>; 2:1). But here outward conflict with persecutors, rather than inward and mental, was what the missionaries had to endure (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.5">Ac 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.30">Php 1:30</reference>). <div eID="gen36627" type="x-p"/>
entries.060679ea28572209685553bf18497f8feefd1663: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17932"/><div sID="gen36628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17932"/><hi type="bold">3. For--</hi>The ground of his "boldness" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1Th 2:2</reference>), his freedom from all "deceit, uncleanness, and guile"; guile, before God, deceit (Greek, "imposture"), towards men (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Co 1:12</reference>; 2:17; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>); uncleanness, in relation to one's self (impure motives of carnal self-gratification in gain, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">1Th 2:5</reference>), or lust; such as actuated false teachers of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.16">Php 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.10">2Pe 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>; Jude 8; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.14">Re 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>). So Simon Magus and Cerinthus taught [Estius].<div eID="gen36628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exhortation--</hi>The Greek means "consolation" as well as "exhortation." The same Gospel which exhorts comforts. Its first lesson to each is that of peace in believing amidst outward and inward sorrows. It comforts them that mourn (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.11">1Th 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Is 61:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.3">2Co 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen36629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>springing from--having its source in--deceit, &c. <div eID="gen36630" type="x-p"/>
entries.de273155b2b8901e718722ebc85edcc2687eff90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17933"/><div sID="gen36631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17933"/><hi type="bold">4. as--</hi>according as; even as.<div eID="gen36631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">allowed--</hi>Greek, "We have been approved on trial," "deemed fit." This word corresponds to "God which trieth our hearts" below. This approval as to sincerity depends solely on the grace and mercy of God (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.15">Ac 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.25">1Co 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2Co 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.11">1Ti 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen36632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not as pleasing--</hi>not as persons who seek to please men; characteristic of false teachers (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>). <div eID="gen36633" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bf041d0cddf1f9ce14fe9d6305a63da8cefc55e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17934"/><div sID="gen36634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17934"/><hi type="bold">5. used we flattering words--</hi>literally, "become (that is, have we been found) in (the use of) language of flattery"; the resource of those who try to "please men."<div eID="gen36634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ye know--</hi>"Ye know" as to whether I flattered you; as to "covetousness," God, the Judge of the heart, alone can be "my witness."<div eID="gen36635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cloak of--</hi>that is, any specious guise under which I might cloak "covetousness." <div eID="gen36636" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fc3a6a422bb467257a7a051cda2303f012f64b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17935"/><div sID="gen36637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17935"/>6. Literally, "Nor of men (have we been found, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">1Th 2:5</reference>) seeking glory." The "of" here represents a different Greek word from "of" in the clause "of you ... of others." Alford makes the former (Greek, "ex") express the abstract ground of the glory; the latter (apo) the concrete object from which it was to come. The former means "originating from"; the latter means "on the part of." Many teach heretical novelties, though not for fain, yet for "glory." Paul and his associates were free even from this motive [Grotius], (<reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>).<div eID="gen36637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we might have been burdensome--</hi>that is, by claiming maintenance (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>). As, however, "glory" precedes, as well as "covetousness," the reference cannot be restricted to the latter, though I think it is not excluded. Translate, "when we might have borne heavily upon you," by pressing you with the weight of self-glorifying authority, and with the burden of our sustenance. Thus the antithesis is appropriate in the words following, "But we were gentle (the opposite of pressing weightily) among you" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.7">1Th 2:7</reference>). On weight being connected with authority, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>, "His letters are weighty" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.21">1Co 4:21</reference>). Alford's translation, which excludes reference to his right of claiming maintenance ("when we might have stood on our dignity"), seems to me disproved by <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>, which uses the same Greek word unequivocally for "chargeable." Twice he received supplies from Philippi while at Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">Php 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen36638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the apostles--</hi>that is, as being apostles. <div eID="gen36639" type="x-p"/>
entries.f179646db3dacb6c1020294d97778f79a7521af2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17936"/><div sID="gen36640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17936"/><hi type="bold">7. we were--</hi>Greek, "we were made" by God's grace.<div eID="gen36640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gentle--</hi>Greek, "mild in bearing with the faults of others" [Tittmann]; one, too, who is gentle (though firm) in reproving the erroneous opinions of others (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>). Some of the oldest manuscripts read, "we became little children" (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.18.3">Mt 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.4">4</reference>). Others support the English Version reading, which forms a better antithesis to <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.6">1Th 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>, and harmonizes better with what follows; for he would hardly, in the same sentence, compare himself both to the "infants" or "little children," and to "a nurse," or rather, "suckling mother." Gentleness is the fitting characteristic of a nurse.<div eID="gen36641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among you--</hi>Greek, "in the midst of you," that is, in our intercourse with you being as one of yourselves.<div eID="gen36642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nurse--</hi>a suckling mother.<div eID="gen36643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36644" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her--</hi>Greek, "her own children" (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.11">1Th 2:11</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>. <div eID="gen36644" type="x-p"/>
entries.22ca11e8c0e09f1780e6470c28a356b17f6f31f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17937"/><div sID="gen36645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17937"/><hi type="bold">8. So--</hi>to be joined to "we were willing"; "As a nurse cherisheth ... so we were willing," &c. [Alford]. But Bengel, "So," that is, seeing that we have such affection for you.<div eID="gen36645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being affectionately desirous--</hi>The oldest reading in the Greek implies, literally, to connect one's self with another; to be closely attached to another.<div eID="gen36646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">willing--</hi>The Greek is stronger, "we were well content"; "we would gladly have imparted," &c. "even our own lives" (so the Greek for "souls" ought to be translated); as we showed in the sufferings we endured in giving you the Gospel (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.1-Acts.17.34">Ac 17:1-34</reference>). As a nursing mother is ready to impart not only her milk to them, but her life for them, so we not only imparted gladly the spiritual milk of the word to you, but risked our own lives for your spiritual nourishment, imitating Him who laid down His life for His friends, the greatest proof of love (<reference osisRef="John.15.13">Joh 15:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36648" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye were--</hi>Greek, "ye were become," as having become our spiritual children.<div eID="gen36648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dear--</hi>Greek, "dearly beloved." <div eID="gen36649" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbffacfa466c1acbd9332dcf0394d5e27e03a988: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17938"/><div sID="gen36650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17938"/><hi type="bold">9. labour and travail--</hi>The Greek for "labor" means hardship in bearing; that for "travail," hardship in doing; the former, toil with the utmost solicitude; the latter, the being wearied with fatigue [Grotius]. Zanchius refers the former to spiritual (see <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.5">1Th 3:5</reference>), the latter to manual labor. I would translate, "weariness (so the Greek is translated, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.27">2Co 11:27</reference>) and travail" (hard labor, toil).<div eID="gen36650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen36651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labouring--</hi>Greek, "working," namely, at tent-making (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night and day--</hi>The Jews reckoned the day from sunset to sunset, so that "night" is put before "day" (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">Ac 20:31</reference>). Their labors with their hands for a scanty livelihood had to be engaged in not only by day, but by night also, in the intervals between spiritual labors.<div eID="gen36653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because we would not be chargeable--</hi>Greek, "with a view to not burdening any of you" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen36654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preached unto you--</hi>Greek, "unto and among you." Though but "three Sabbaths" are mentioned, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>, these refer merely to the time of his preaching to the Jews in the synagogue. When rejected by them as a body, after having converted a few Jews, he turned to the Gentiles; of these (whom he preached to in a place distinct from the synagogue) "a great multitude believed" (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.4">Ac 17:4</reference>, where the oldest manuscripts read, "of the devout [proselytes] and Greeks a great multitude"); then after he had, by labors continued among the Gentiles for some time, gathered in many converts, the Jews, provoked by his success, assaulted Jason's house, and drove him away. His receiving "once and again" supplies from Philippi, implies a longer stay at Thessalonica than three weeks (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">Php 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen36655" type="x-p"/>
entries.17bd796274d7529324059173e33f7d09190e843e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17939"/><div sID="gen36656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17939"/><hi type="bold">10. Ye are witnesses--</hi>as to our outward conduct.<div eID="gen36656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God--</hi>as to our inner motives.<div eID="gen36657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holily--</hi>towards God.<div eID="gen36658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justly--</hi>towards men.<div eID="gen36659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unblamably--</hi>in relation to ourselves.<div eID="gen36660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behaved ourselves--</hi>Greek, "were made to be," namely, by God.<div eID="gen36661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among you that believe--</hi>rather, "before (that is, in the eyes of) you that believe"; whatever we may have seemed in the eyes of the unbelieving. As <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference> refers to their outward occupation in the world; so <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.10">1Th 2:10</reference>, to their character among believers. <div eID="gen36662" type="x-p"/>
entries.82790732ab15347cf1f6464e197f64d91762391b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17940"/><div sID="gen36663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17940"/><hi type="bold">11. exhorted and comforted--</hi>Exhortation leads one to do a thing willingly; consolation, to do it joyfully [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.14">1Th 5:14</reference>). Even in the former term, "exhorted," the Greek includes the additional idea of comforting and advocating one's cause: "encouragingly exhorted." Appropriate in this case, as the Thessalonians were in sorrow, both through persecutions, and also through deaths of friends (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charged--</hi>"conjured solemnly," literally, "testifying"; appealing solemnly to you before God.<div eID="gen36664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one of you--</hi>in private (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.20">Ac 20:20</reference>), as well as publicly. The minister, if he would be useful, must not deal merely in generalities, but must individualize and particularize.<div eID="gen36665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a father--</hi>with mild gravity. The Greek is, "his own children." <div eID="gen36666" type="x-p"/>
entries.de4d8c8c2b1ca5ba8065c66325b76d84f6842441: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17941"/><div sID="gen36667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17941"/><hi type="bold">12. worthy of God--</hi>"worthy of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.10">Col 1:10</reference>); "worthily of the saints" (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.2">Ro 16:2</reference>, Greek): "... of the Gospel" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.27">Php 1:27</reference>) "... of the vocation wherewith ye are called" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>). Inconsistency would cause God's name to be "blasphemed among the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Ro 2:24</reference>). The Greek article is emphatical, "Worthy of THE God who is calling you."<div eID="gen36667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath called--</hi>So one of the oldest manuscripts and Vulgate. Other oldest manuscripts, "Who calleth us."<div eID="gen36668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his kingdom--</hi>to be set up at the Lord's coming.<div eID="gen36669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>that ye may share His glory (<reference osisRef="John.17.22">Joh 17:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen36670" type="x-p"/>
entries.caf1f3a85d0e494a9405ea099d03b9ffa0a13013: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17942"/><div sID="gen36671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17942"/><hi type="bold">13. For this cause--</hi>Seeing ye have had such teachers (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.10-1Thess.2.12">1Th 2:10-12</reference>) [Bengel], "we also (as well as 'all that believe' in Macedonia and Achaia) thank God without ceasing ('always' ... 'in our prayers,' <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.2">1Th 1:2</reference>), that when ye received the word of God which ye heard from us (literally, 'God's word of hearing from us,' <reference osisRef="Rom.10.16">Ro 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">17</reference>), ye accepted it not as the word of men, but, even as it is truly, the word of God." Alford omits the "as" of English Version. But the "as" is required by the clause, "even as it is truly." "Ye accepted it, not (as) the word of men (which it might have been supposed to be), but (as) the word of God, even as it really is." The Greek for the first "received," implies simply the hearing of it; the Greek of the second is "accepted," or "welcomed" it. The proper object of faith, it hence appears, is the word of God, at first oral, then for security against error, written (<reference osisRef="John.20.30">Joh 20:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.4">Ro 15:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.30">Ga 4:30</reference>). Also, that faith is the work of divine grace, is implied by Paul's thanksgiving.<div eID="gen36671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">effectually worketh also in you that believe--</hi>"Also," besides your accepting it with your hearts, it evidences itself in your lives. It shows its energy in its practical effects on you; for instance, working in you patient endurance in trial (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.14">1Th 2:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.3.5">Ga 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen36672" type="x-p"/>
entries.2acfe6339075c758c68bda84dcd5c6a37c67f1b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17943"/><div sID="gen36673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17943"/><hi type="bold">14. followers--</hi>Greek, "imitators." Divine working is most of all seen and felt in affliction.<div eID="gen36673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Judea--</hi>The churches of Judea were naturally the patterns to other churches, as having been the first founded, and that on the very scene of Christ's own ministry. Reference to them is specially appropriate here, as the Thessalonians, with Paul and Silas, had experienced from Jews in their city persecutions (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.5-Acts.17.9">Ac 17:5-9</reference>) similar to those which "the churches in Judea" experienced from Jews in that country.<div eID="gen36674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ Jesus--</hi>not merely "in God"; for the synagogues of the Jews (one of which the Thessalonians were familiar with, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.1">Ac 17:1</reference>) were also in God. But the Christian churches alone were not only in God, as the Jews in contrast to the Thessalonian idolaters were, but also in Christ, which the Jews were not.<div eID="gen36675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of your own countrymen--</hi>including primarily the Jews settled at Thessalonica, from whom the persecution originated, and also the Gentiles there, instigated by the Jews; thus, "fellow countrymen" (the Greek term, according to Herodian, implies, not the enduring relation of fellow citizenship, but sameness of country for the time being), including naturalized Jews and native Thessalonians, stand in contrast to the pure "Jews" in Judea (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">Mt 10:36</reference>). It is an undesigned coincidence, that Paul at this time was suffering persecutions of the Jews at Corinth, whence he writes (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Ac 18:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.12">6, 12</reference>); naturally his letter would the more vividly dwell on Jewish bitterness against Christians.<div eID="gen36676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even as they--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.10.32-Heb.10.34">He 10:32-34</reference>). There was a likeness in respect to the nation from which both suffered, namely, Jews, and those their own countrymen; in the cause for which, and in the evils which, they suffered, and also in the steadfast manner in which they suffered them. Such sameness of fruits, afflictions, and experimental characteristics of believers, in all places and at all times, is a subsidiary evidence of the truth of the Gospel. <div eID="gen36677" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd33f3794c26575ee78f47d0dce536702a8e3187: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17944"/><div sID="gen36678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17944"/><hi type="bold">15. the Lord Jesus--</hi>rather as Greek, "Jesus THE Lord." This enhances the glaring enormity of their sin, that in killing Jesus they killed the Lord (Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.3.14">Ac 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen36678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen36679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophets--</hi>(Mt 21:33-41; 23:31-37; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.33">Lu 13:33</reference>).<div eID="gen36680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">persecuted us--</hi>rather as Greek (see Margin), "By persecution drove us out" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.49">Lu 11:49</reference>).<div eID="gen36681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">please not God--</hi>that is, they do not make it their aim to please God. He implies that with all their boast of being God's peculiar people, they all the while are "no pleasers of God," as certainly as, by the universal voice of the world, which even they themselves cannot contradict, they are declared to be perversely "contrary to all men." Josephus [Against Apion, 2.14], represents one calling them "Atheists and Misanthropes, the dullest of barbarians"; and Tacitus [Histories, 5.5], "They have a hostile hatred of all other men." However, the contrariety to all men here meant is, in that they "forbid us to speak to the Gentiles that they may be saved" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1Th 2:16</reference>). <div eID="gen36682" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7ff5a7f417e3ca5f98bdb8663dd77ef851e0a1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17945"/><div sID="gen36683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17945"/><hi type="bold">16. Forbidding--</hi>Greek, "Hindering us from speaking," &c.<div eID="gen36683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to fill up their sins alway--</hi>Tending thus "to the filling up (the full measure of, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Ge 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">Da 8:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Mt 23:32</reference>) their sins at all times," that is, now as at all former times. Their hindrance of the Gospel preaching to the Gentiles was the last measure added to their continually accumulating iniquity, which made them fully ripe for vengeance.<div eID="gen36684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>Greek, "but." "But," they shall proceed no further, for (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2Ti 3:8</reference>) "the" divine "wrath has (so the Greek) come upon (overtaken unexpectedly; the past tense expressing the speedy certainty of the divinely destined stroke) them to the uttermost"; not merely partial wrath, but wrath to its full extent, "even to the finishing stroke" [Edmunds]. The past tense implies that the fullest visitation of wrath was already begun. Already in A.D. 48, a tumult had occurred at the Passover in Jerusalem, when about thirty thousand (according to some) were slain; a foretaste of the whole vengeance which speedily followed (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.43">Lu 19:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.44">44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.24">21:24</reference>). <div eID="gen36685" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9f8c62d88a3a8ce2ffc4a56fcbb8b968b3ed96a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17946"/><div sID="gen36686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17946"/><hi type="bold">17. But we--</hi>resumed from <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1Th 2:13</reference>; in contrast to the Jews, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1Th 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>.<div eID="gen36686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken--</hi>rather as Greek, "severed (violently, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.7-Acts.17.10">Ac 17:7-10</reference>) from you," as parents bereft of their children. So "I will not leave you comfortless," Greek, "orphanized" (<reference osisRef="John.14.18">Joh 14:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a short time--</hi>literally, "for the space of an hour." "When we had been severed from you but a very short time (perhaps alluding to the suddenness of his unexpected departure), we the more abundantly (the shorter was our separation; for the desire of meeting again is the more vivid, the more recent has been the parting) endeavored," &c. (Compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.4">2Ti 1:4</reference>). He does not hereby, as many explain, anticipate a short separation from them, which would be a false anticipation; for he did not soon revisit them. The Greek past participle also forbids their view. <div eID="gen36688" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a8f08991e85531c77c171db36a20fb359df58bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17947"/><div sID="gen36689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17947"/><hi type="bold">18. Wherefore--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Because," or "Inasmuch as."<div eID="gen36689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we would--</hi>Greek, "we wished to come"; we intended to come.<div eID="gen36690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even I Paul--</hi>My fellow missionaries as well as myself wished to come; I can answer for myself that I intended it more than once. His slightly distinguishing himself here from his fellow missionaries, whom throughout this Epistle he associates with himself in the plural, accords with the fact that Silvanus and Timothy stayed at Berea when Paul went on to Athens; where subsequently Timothy joined him, and was thence sent by Paul alone to Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Satan hindered us--</hi>On a different occasion "the Holy Ghost, the Spirit of Jesus" (so the oldest manuscripts read), <reference osisRef="Acts.16.6">Ac 16:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.7">7</reference>, forbad or hindered them in a missionary design; here it is Satan, acting perhaps by wicked men, some of whom had already driven him out of Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.13">Ac 17:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.14">14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.13.27">Joh 13:27</reference>), or else by some more direct "messenger of Satan--a thorn in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.14">2Co 11:14</reference>). In any event, the Holy Ghost and the providence of God overruled Satan's opposition to further His own purpose. We cannot, in each case, define whence hindrances in good undertakings arise; Paul in this case, by inspiration, was enabled to say; the hindrance was from Satan. Grotius thinks Satan's mode of hindering Paul's journey to Thessalonica was by instigating the Stoic and Epicurean philosophers to cavil, which entailed on Paul the necessity of replying, and so detained him; but he seems to have left Athens leisurely (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.33">Ac 17:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.1">18:1</reference>). The Greek for "hindered" is literally, "to cut a trench between one's self and an advancing foe, to prevent his progress"; so Satan opposing the progress of the missionaries. <div eID="gen36692" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a5c37ab958d9641144de2587481b4cd6c3610e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17948"/><div sID="gen36693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17948"/><hi type="bold">19. For--</hi>giving the reason for his earnest desire to see them.<div eID="gen36693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Are not even ye in the presence of ... Christ--</hi>"Christ" is omitted in the oldest manuscripts. Are not even ye (namely, among others; the "even" or "also," implies that not they alone will be his crown) our hope, joy, and crown of rejoicing before Jesus, when He shall come (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.14">2Co 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.16">Php 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>)? The "hope" here meant is his hope (in a lower sense), that these his converts might be found in Christ at His advent (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>). Paul's chief "hope" was Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1Ti 1:1</reference>). <div eID="gen36694" type="x-p"/>
entries.1daaa512e5188c3416d246ba854d9fdba50ddcb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17949"/><div sID="gen36695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17949"/>20. Emphatical repetition with increased force. Who but ye and our other converts are our hope, &c., hereafter, at Christ's coming? For it is ye who ARE now our glory and joy. <chapter eID="1Thess.2"/>

entries.06e0e669cf4011946d6352801b3f389346d125bd: <div eID="gen51084" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51085" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51086" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51086" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51085" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51087" type="x-p"/> The apostle sets forth how the Gospel was brought and preached to the Thessalonians, in consequence of his being persecuted at Philippi, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.1">1Thes 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.2">1Thes 2:2</reference>. The manner in which the apostles preached, the matter of their doctrine, and the tenor of their lives, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.3-1Thes.2.11">1Thes 2:3-11</reference>. He exhorts them to walk worthy of God, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.12">1Thes 2:12</reference>. And commends them for the manner in which they received the Gospel, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.13">1Thes 2:13</reference>. How they suffered from their own countrymen, as the first believers did from the Jews, who endeavored to prevent the apostles from preaching the Gospel to the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.14-1Thes.2.16">1Thes 2:14-16</reference>. St. Paul's apology for his absence from them; and his earnest desire to see them, founded on his great affection for them, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.17-1Thes.2.20">1Thes 2:17-20</reference>. <div eID="gen51087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51088" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51089" type="x-p"/> Our entrance in unto you - His first coming to preach the Gospel was particularly owned of the Lord, many of them having been converted under his ministry. This consideration gave him a right to deliver all the following exhortations.
entries.9d70b509c8837ce30e0e89711b329f71babff8fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51090" type="x-p"/> Shamefully entreated - at Philippi - There Paul and Silas had been beaten with many stripes, shut up in the inner prison, and their feet made fast in the stocks. See <reference osisRef="Act.16.23">Act 16:23</reference>, etc.; and the notes there. <div eID="gen51090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51091" type="x-p"/> With much contention - The words εν πολλῳ αγωνι not only signify, with intense labor and earnestness, but may here mean, exposed to the greatest danger; at the peril of our lives. The Greek phrase quoted by Rosenmuller is to the point, αγων προφασιν ουκ αναμενει, in danger we must not delay - activity and despatch are then indispensably necessary.
entries.d01acb68fdd24c8228376beae44317435bcf4635: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51092" type="x-p"/> Our exhortation - The word παρακλησιςhas a very extensive meaning; it signifies not only exhortation and teaching in general, but also encouragement, consolation, and the like. When the apostles exhorted or admonished men, it was that they should turn from evil to good, from misery to happiness, from Satan to God, and from hell to heaven. Their exhortations having this object, every word was consolatory; and as the truth which they delivered was unquestionable, therefore their ministry was a subject of the highest encouragement and joy. <div eID="gen51092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51093" type="x-p"/> Not of deceit - We did not endeavor to allure you with false pretences; we did not deceive you, nor were we deceived ourselves. <div eID="gen51093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51094" type="x-p"/> Nor of uncleanness - Such as the teachings of the Gentile philosophers were; their supreme gods were celebrated for their adulteries, fornications, uncleannesses, thefts, barbarities, and profligacies of the most odious kind. Our Gospel was pure; came from the pure and holy God; was accompanied with the influences of the Holy Spirit, and produced purity both in the hearts and lives of all that received it. <div eID="gen51094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51095" type="x-p"/> Nor in guile - We had no false pretences, and were influenced by no sinister motives.
entries.d8ae4114c6b9715d6b547bf02aa7ce55cbfac470: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51096" type="x-p"/> But as we were allowed of God - Καθως δεδοκιμασμεθα· As we were accounted worthy to be put in trust - as God put confidence in us, and sent us on his most especial message to mankind, even so we speak, keeping the dignity of our high calling continually in view; and, acting as in the sight of God, we speak not to please or flatter men, though our doctrine is the most consolatory that can be conceived, but to please that God who searcheth the heart, and before whom all our motives are constantly without a veil.
entries.aad204a0289472b10039ea17021204b428b8f7c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51097" type="x-p"/> Flattering words - Though we proclaimed the Gospel or glad tidings, yet we showed that without holiness none should see the Lord. <div eID="gen51097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51098" type="x-p"/> Ye know - That while we preached the whole Gospel we never gave any countenance to sin. <div eID="gen51098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51099" type="x-p"/> For a cloak of covetousness - We did not seek temporal emolument; nor did we preach the Gospel for a cloak to our covetousness: God is witness that we did not; we sought you, not yours. Hear this, ye that preach the Gospel! Can ye call God to witness that in preaching it ye have no end in view by your ministry but his glory in the salvation of souls? Or do ye enter into the priesthood for a morsel of bread, or for what is ominously and impiously called a living, a benefice? In better days your place and office were called a cure of souls; what care have you for the souls of them by whose labors you are in general more than sufficiently supported? Is it your study, your earnest labor, to bring sinners to God; to preach among your heathen parishioners the unsearchable riches of Christ? <div eID="gen51099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51100" type="x-p"/> But I should speak to the thousands who have no parishes, but who have their chapels, their congregations, pew and seat rents, etc., etc. Is it for the sake of these that ye have entered or continue in the Gospel ministry? Is God witness that, in all these things, ye have no cloak of covetousness? Happy is the man who can say so, whether he has the provision which the law of the land allows him, or whether he lives on the free-will offerings of the people. <div eID="gen51100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51101" type="x-p"/> The faithful laborer is worthy of his hire; for the ox that treads out the corn should not be muzzled; and they that preach the Gospel should live, not riot, by the Gospel. But wo to that man who enters into the labor for the sake of the hire! he knows not Christ; and how can he preach him?
entries.3eaf42543e95574f65e0ce1714b632fd5e76293d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51102" type="x-p"/> Nor of men sought we glory - As we preached not for worldly gain, so we preached not for popular applause; we had what we sought for-the approbation of God, and the testimony of a good conscience. <div eID="gen51102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51103" type="x-p"/> When we might have been burdensome - They had a right to their maintenance while they devoted themselves wholly to the work of the Gospel for the sake of the people's souls. Others understand the words εν βαρει ειναι, to be honorable; we sought no glory of you nor of others, though we were honorable as the apostles of Christ. כבוד cabod, in Hebrew, to which the Greek βαρος answers, signifies not only weight but glory; and in both these senses the apostle uses it, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2Cor 4:17</reference>.
entries.f34cb02f0074678813959656288a077ee775e608: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51104" type="x-p"/> But we were gentle among you - Far from assuming the authority which we had, we acted towards you as a tender nurse or parent does to a delicate child. We fed, counselled, cherished, and bore with you; we taught you to walk, preserved you from stumbling, and led you in a right path. <div eID="gen51104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51105" type="x-p"/> Instead of ηπιοι, gentle, many MSS., and several versions and fathers, have νηπιοι, young children. But this never can be considered the original reading, the scope of the place being totally opposed to it. It is the Thessalonians whom the apostle considers as young children, and himself and fellow laborers as the nurse; he could with no propriety say that he was among them as a little child, while himself professed to be their nurse.
entries.5ca605fd274dab1ff54741c169403ad7c639c9fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51106" type="x-p"/> Being affectionately desirous of you - We had such intense love for you that we were not only willing and forward to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ to you, but also to give our own lives for your sake, because ye were dear, διοτι αγαπητοι ἡμιν, because ye were beloved by us. The words used here by the apostle are expressive of the strongest affection and attachment.
entries.9b1ef03fc28d91a791f35787087eb83ddfd77513: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51107" type="x-p"/> Ye remember - our labor and travail - From this it appears that St. Paul spent much more time at Thessalonica than is generally supposed; for the expressions in this verse denote a long continuance of a constantly exercised ministry, interrupted only by manual labor for their own support; labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable to you. Probably Paul and his companions worked with their hands by day, and spent a considerable part of the night, or evenings, in preaching Christ to the people.
entries.7cd2065f600394ed1f28925c97c58bc40c01ee6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51108" type="x-p"/> Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily - i.e., in reference to God; how justly in reference to men; and unblamably in reference to our spirit and conduct, as ministers of Christ, we behaved ourselves among you. What a consciousness of his own integrity must St. Paul have had to use the expressions that are here! No hypocrite, and none who did the work of the Lord carelessly, could make such an appeal both to God and man.
entries.03bbec8c16492370b8d594c3c157292d6df0a342: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen51108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51109" type="x-p"/> How we exhorted - What pastoral care is marked here! They exhorted - were continually teaching and instructing, the objects of their charge; this was their general work. <div eID="gen51109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51110" type="x-p"/> And comforted - They found many under trials and temptations, and those they encouraged. <div eID="gen51110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51111" type="x-p"/> And charged - Μαρτυρουμενοι· Continued witness to the people that all the threatenings and promises of God were true; that he required faith, love, and obedience; that he could not behold sin with allowance; that Jesus died to save them from their sins; and that, without holiness, none should see God. And all these things they did, not in a general way only, but they spoke to every man; none was left unnoticed, unadmonished, uncomforted. The spirit in which they performed all these branches of the pastoral care was that which was most likely to insure success; as a father treats his children, so they treated every member of the Church.
entries.25cb82640c776acbfd590d6fb25d156773fd4bbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen51111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51112" type="x-p"/> That ye would walk worthy of God - That they should, in every respect, act up to their high calling, that it would not be a reproach to the God of holiness to acknowledge them as his sons and daughters. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Eph 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phi.1.27">Phi 1:27</reference> (note); and <reference osisRef="Col.1.10">Col 1:10</reference> (note). <div eID="gen51112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51113" type="x-p"/> His Kingdom and glory - His Church here, for that is the kingdom of God among men; and his glory hereafter, for that is the state to which the dispensations of grace in his Church lead. The words, how ever, may be a hendiadys, and signify his glorious kingdom.
entries.091b7d07255d369a06c8e8a08bc11b54b4a9f9ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen51113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51114" type="x-p"/> Ye received the word of God - Ye received the doctrine of God, not as any thing fabricated by man, but as coming immediately from God himself, we being only his messengers to declare what he had previously revealed to us. And ye have had the fullest proof that ye have not believed in vain; for that doctrine, under the power and influence of the Holy Ghost, has worked most powerfully in you, filling you with light, life, and holiness.
entries.c0592af5b3db91751abb8f3a155196b89cbbb14f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen51114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51115" type="x-p"/> Ye - became followers of the Churches of God - There is not a word here of the Church of Rome being the model after which the other Churches were to be formed; it had no such pre-eminence: this honor belonged to the Churches of Judea; it was according to them, not the Church at Rome, that the Asiatic Churches were modelled.
