But if pious men, whose promptitude Paul so highly commends, stood in absolute need of being stimulated by stirring exhortations, nay, adjurations, what must be done with us, in whom sluggishness
“La paresse et nonchalance de la chair;” — “Indolence and negligence of the flesh.”
of the flesh does more reign? In the mean time, as to the wicked, whose obstinacy is incurable, it is necessary to denounce upon them the horrible vengeance of God, not so much from hope of success, as in order that they may be rendered inexcusable.
Some render the participle παραμυθουμένοι, comforted. If we adopt this rendering, he means that he made use of consolations in dealing with the afflicted, who need to be sustained by the grace of God, and refreshed by tasting of heavenly blessings,
“Fortifiez ou soulagez en leur rafrechissant le goust des biens celestes;” — “Strengthened or comforted in the way of refreshing their taste with heavenly blessings.”
that they may not lose heart or become impatient. The other meaning, however, is more suitable to the context, that he admonished; for the three verbs, it is manifest, refer to the same thing.
That ye might walk. He presents in a few words the sum and substance of his exhortations, that, in magnifying the mercy of God, he admonished them not to fail as to their calling. His commendation of the grace of God is contained in the expression, who hath called us into his kingdom. For as our salvation is founded upon God’s gracious adoption, every blessing that Christ has brought us is comprehended in this one term. It now remains that we answer God’s call, that is, that we shew ourselves to be such children to him as he is a Father to us. For he who lives otherwise than as becomes a child of God, deserves to be cut off from God’s household.
1 Thessalonians 2:13-16
13. For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe.
13 Quapropter nos quoque indesinenter gratias agimus Deo, quod, quum sermonem Dei praedicatum a nobis percepistis, amplexi estis, non ut sermonem hominum, sed quemadmodum revera est, sermonem Dei: qui etiam efficaciter agit in vobis credentibus.
14. For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judea are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews:
14. Vos enim imitatores facti estis, fratres, Ecclesiarum Dei, quae sunt in Iudaea in Christo Iesu: quia eadem passi estis et vos a propriis tribulibus, quemadmodum et ipsi a Iudaeis.
15. Who both killed the Lord Jesus, and their own prophets, and have persecuted us; and they please not God, and are contrary to all men:
15. Qui Dominum Iesum occiderunt, et proprios Prophetas, et nos persequuti sunt, et Deo non placent, et cunctis hominibus adversi sunt:
16. Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved, to fill up their sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost.
16. Qui obsistunt ne Gentibus loquamur, ut salvae fiant, ut compleantur eorum peccata semper: pervenit enim in eos ira usque in finem.
entries.f2f8bb29258eb4c9d8ab3bb16c6672bcdb015f1c: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.2.13" sID="gen128063" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13</hi> <hi type="italic">Wherefore we give thanks</hi>. Having spoken of his ministry, he returns again to address the Thessalonians, that he may always commend that mutual harmony of which he has previously made mention. <note n="537"> <div sID="gen128065" type="x-p"/> Calvin refers here to the harmony which happily subsisted between the preaching of Paul and the faith of the Thessalonians.—<hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen128065" type="x-p"/> </note> He says, therefore, that he gives thanks to God, because they had <hi type="italic">embraced the word of God which they heard from his mouth, as the word of God, as it truly was.</hi> Now, by these expressions he means, that it has been received by them reverently, and with the obedience with which it ought. For so soon as this persuasion has gained a footing, it is impossible but that a feeling of obligation to obey takes possession of our minds. <note n="538"> <div sID="gen128066" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il ne se pent faire que nous ne venions quant et quant a auoir vne saincte affection d’obeir</foreign>;” — “It cannot but be that we come at the same time to have a holy disposition to obey.”<div eID="gen128066" type="x-p"/> </note> For who would not shudder at the thought of resisting God? Who would not regard contempt of God with detestation? The circumstance, therefore, that the word of God is regarded by many with such contempt, that it is scarcely held in any estimation — that many are not at all actuated by fear, arises from this, that they do not consider that they have to do with God.<div eID="gen128064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128067" type="x-p"/>Hence we learn from this passage what credit ought to be given to the gospel — such as does not depend on the authority of men, but, resting on the sure and ascertained truth of God, raises itself above the world; and, in fine, is as far above mere opinion, as heaven is above earth: <note n="539"> <div sID="gen128068" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Aussi lois d’vne opinion, ou d’vn cuider</foreign>;” — “As far above opinion, or imagination.”<div eID="gen128068" type="x-p"/> </note> and, <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, such as produces of itself reverence, fear, and obedience, inasmuch as men, touched with a feeling of Divine majesty, will never allow themselves to sport with it. Teachers <note n="540"> <div sID="gen128069" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les Docteurs, c’est a dire ceux qui ont la charge d’enseigner</foreign>;” — “Teachers, that is to say, those that have the task of instructing.”<div eID="gen128069" type="x-p"/> </note> are, in their turn, admonished to beware of bringing forward anything but the pure word of God, for if this was not allowable for Paul, it will not be so for any one in the present day. He proves, however, from the effect produced, that it was the word of God that he had delivered, inasmuch as it had produced that fruit of heavenly doctrine which the Prophets celebrate, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.55.11 Bible:Isa.55.13">Isaiah 55:11,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.29">Jeremiah 23:29</reference>) in renewing their life, <note n="541"> <div sID="gen128070" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En renouelant et reformant la vie des Thessaloniciens</foreign>;” — “In renewing and reforming the life of the Thessalonians.”<div eID="gen128070" type="x-p"/> </note> for the doctrine of men could accomplish no such thing. The relative pronoun may be taken as referring either to <hi type="italic">God</hi> or to his <hi type="italic">word</hi>, but whichever way you choose, the meaning will come all to one, for as the Thessalonians felt in themselves a Divine energy, which proceeded from faith, they might rest assured that what they had heard was not a mere sound of the human voice vanishing into air, but the living and efficacious doctrine of God.<div eID="gen128067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128071" type="x-p"/>As to the expression, <hi type="italic">the word of the preaching of God</hi>, it means simply, as I have rendered it, <hi type="italic">the word of God preached by man.</hi> For Paul meant to state expressly that they had not looked upon the doctrine as contemptible, although it had proceeded from the mouth of a mortal man, inasmuch as they recognized God as the author of it. He accordingly praises the Thessalonians, because they did not rest in mere regard for the minister. but lifted up their eyes to God, that they might receive his word. Accordingly, I have not hesitated to insert the particle <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">ut</hi></foreign>, (<hi type="italic">that</hi>,) which served to make the meaning more clear. There is a mistake on the part of Erasmus in rendering it, “the word of the hearing of God,” as if Paul meant that God had been manifested. He afterwards changed it thus, “the word by which you learned God,” for he did not advert to the Hebrew idiom. <note n="542"> <div sID="gen128072" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car il n’a pas prins garde que c’estoit yci vne façon de parler prinse de la langue Hebraique</foreign>;” — “For he did not take notice that it was a manner of expression taken from the Hebrew language.”<div eID="gen128072" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen128071" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128063" osisID="1Thess.2.13" type="section"/>
entries.123d6147458d1718f50abee3f8c97c727fa2f125: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.2.14" sID="gen128073" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14</hi> <hi type="italic">For ye became imitators</hi>. If you are inclined to restrict this to the clause in immediate connection with it, the meaning will be, that the power of God, or of his word, shews itself in their patient endurance, while they sustain persecutions with magnanimity and undaunted courage. I prefer, however, to view it as extending to the whole of the foregoing statement, for he confirms what he has stated, that the Thessalonians had in good earnest embraced the gospel, as being presented to them by God, inasmuch as they courageously endured the assaults which Satan made upon them, and did not refuse to suffer anything rather than leave off obedience to it. And, unquestionably, this is no slight test of faith when Satan, by all his machinations, has no success in moving us away from the fear of God.<div eID="gen128074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128075" type="x-p"/>In the mean time, he prudently provides against a dangerous temptation which might prostrate or harass them; for they endured grievous troubles from that nation which was the only one in the world that gloried in the name of God.<div eID="gen128075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128076" type="x-p"/>This, I say, might occur to their minds: “If this is the true religion, why do the Jews, who are the sacred people of God, oppose it with such inveterate hostility?” With the view of removing this occasion of offense, <note n="543"> <div sID="gen128077" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Aux Thessaloniciens</foreign>;” — “To the Thessalonians.”<div eID="gen128077" type="x-p"/> </note> he, in the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place, shews them that they have this in common with the first <hi type="italic">Churches that were in Judea:</hi> afterwards, he says that the Jews are determined enemies of God and of all sound doctrine. For although, when he says that they suffered from <hi type="italic">their own countrymen</hi>, this may be explained as referring to others rather than to the Jews, or at least ought not to be restricted to the Jews exclusively, yet as he insists farther in describing their obstinacy and impiety, it is manifest that these same persons are adverted to by him from the beginning. It is probable, that at Thessalonica some from that nation were converted to Christ. It appears, however, from the narrative furnished in the Acts, that <hi type="italic">there</hi>, no less than in Judea, the Jews were persecutors of the gospel. I accordingly take this as being said indiscriminately of Jews as well as of Gentiles, inasmuch as both endured great conflicts and fierce attacks from <hi type="italic">their own countrymen</hi><div eID="gen128076" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128073" osisID="1Thess.2.14" type="section"/>
entries.9def7fe27747aa09c808201dd93784213ed14b91: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.2.15" sID="gen128078" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15</hi> <hi type="italic">Who killed the Lord Jesus</hi>. As that people had been distinguished by so many benefits from God, in consequence of the glory of the ancient fathers, the very name <note n="544"> <div sID="gen128080" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De Juif</foreign>;” — “Of Jew.”<div eID="gen128080" type="x-p"/> </note> was of great authority among many. Lest this disguise should dazzle the eyes of any one, he strips the Jews of all honor, so as to leave them nothing but odium and the utmost infamy.<div eID="gen128079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128081" type="x-p"/>“Behold,” says he, “the virtues for which they deserve praise among the good and pious! — they killed their own prophets and at last the Son of God, they have persecuted me his servant, they wage war with God, they are detested by the whole world, they are hostile to the salvation of the Gentiles; in fine, they are destined to everlasting destruction.”<div eID="gen128081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128082" type="x-p"/>It is asked, why he says that Christ and the prophets were killed by the same persons? I answer, that this refers to the entire body, <note n="545"> <div sID="gen128083" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A tout le corps du peuple</foreign>;” — “To the whole body of the people.”<div eID="gen128083" type="x-p"/> </note> for Paul means that there is nothing new or unusual in their resisting God, but that, on the contrary, they are, in this manner, <hi type="italic">filling up the measure of their fathers</hi>, as Christ speaks. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.32">Matthew 23:32</reference>)<div eID="gen128082" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128078" osisID="1Thess.2.15" type="section"/>

16 Who hinder us from speaking to the Gentiles. It is not without good reason that, as has been observed, he enters so much into detail in exposing the malice of the Jews.
“Il insiste si longuement a deschiffrer et toucher au vif la malice des Juifs;” — “He insists to so great a length in distinctly unfolding and touching to the quick the malice of the Jews.”
For as they furiously opposed the Gospel everywhere, there arose from this a great stumblingblock, more especially as they exclaimed that the gospel was profaned by Paul, when he published it among the Gentiles. By this calumny they made divisions in the Churches, they took away from the Gentiles the hope of salvation, and they obstructed the progress of the gospel. Paul, accordingly, charges them with this crime — that they regard the salvation of the Gentiles with envy, but adds, that matters are so, in order that their sins may be filled up, that he may take away from them all reputation for piety; just as in saying previously, that they pleased not God, (1 Thessalonians 2:15) he meant, that they were unworthy to be reckoned among the worshippers of God. The manner of expression, however, must be observed, implying that those who persevere in an evil course fill up by this means the measure of their judgment,
“Et condemnation;” — “And condemnation.”
until they come to make it a heap. This is the reason why the punishment of the wicked is often delayed — because their impieties, so to speak, are not yet ripe. By this we are warned that we must carefully take heed lest, in the event of our adding from time to time
“Chacun iour;” — “Every day.”
sin to sin, as is wont to happen generally, the heap at last reaches as high as heaven.
For wrath has come. He means that they are in an utterly hopeless state, inasmuch as they are vessels of the Lord’s wrath. “The just vengeance of God presses upon them and pursues them, and will not leave them until they perish — as is the case with all the reprobate, who rush on headlong to death, to which they are destined.” The Apostle, however, makes this declaration as to the entire body of the people, in such a manner as not to deprive the elect of hope. For as the greater proportion resisted Christ, he speaks, it is true, of the whole nation generally, but we must keep in view the exception which he himself makes in Romans 11:5, — that the Lord will always have some seed remaining. We must always keep in view Paul’s design — that believers must carefully avoid the society of those whom the just vengeance of God pursues, until they perish in their blind obstinacy. Wrath, without any additional term, means the judgment of God, as in Romans 4:15, — the law worketh wrath; also in Romans 12:19, — neither give place unto wrath
1 Thessalonians 2:17-20
17. But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire.
17. Nos vero, fratres, orbati vobis ad tempus horae
“Pour vn moment du temps;” — “For a moment of time.”
aspectu, non corde, abundantius studuimus faciem vestram videre in multo desiderio.
18. Wherefore we would have come unto you, even I Paul, once and again; but Satan hindered us.
18. Itaque voluimus venire ad vos, ego quidem Paulus, et semel et bis, et obstitit nobis Satan.
19. For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Are not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?
19. Quae enim nostra spes, vel gaudium, vel corona gloriationis? annon etiam vos coram Domino nostro Iesu Christo in eius adventu?
20. For ye are our glory and joy.
20. Vos enim estis gloria nostra et gaudium.
entries.842651e94839f1f49cd4ecdb708fc3ae81d78102: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.2.17" sID="gen128102" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17</hi> <hi type="italic">But we, brethren, bereaved of you</hi>. This excuse has been appropriately added, lest the Thessalonians should think that Paul had deserted them while so great an emergency demanded his presence. He has spoken of the persecutions which they endured from their own people: he, in the mean time, whose duty it was above all others to assist them, was absent. He has formerly called himself a <hi type="italic">father;</hi> now, it is not the part of a <hi type="italic">father</hi> to desert his children in the midst of such distresses. He, accordingly, obviates all suspicion of contempt and negligence, by saying, that it was from no want of inclination, but because he had not opportunity. Nor does he say simply, “I was desirous to come to you, but my way was obstructed;” but by the peculiar terms that he employs he expresses the intensity of his affection: “When,” says he, “I was <hi type="italic">bereaved</hi> of you.” <note n="550"> <div sID="gen128104" type="x-p"/> “The original word is here very emphatical. It is an allusion to that grief, anxiety, and reluctance of heart, with which dying, affectionate parents take leave of their own children, when they are just going to leave them helpless orphans, exposed to the injuries of a merciless and wicked world, or that sorrow of heart with which poor destitute orphans close the eyes of their dying parents.” —<hi type="italic">Benson</hi>.—<hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen128104" type="x-p"/> </note> By the word <hi type="italic">bereaved</hi>, he declares how sad and distressing a thing it was to him to be absent from them. <note n="551"> <div sID="gen128105" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le mot Grec signifie l’estat d’vn pere qui a perdu ses enfans, ou des enfans qui ont perdu leur pere</foreign>;” — “The Greek word denotes the condition of a father that has lost his children, or of children that have lost their father.”<div eID="gen128105" type="x-p"/> </note> This is followed by a fuller expression of his feeling of desire — that it was with difficulty that he could endure their absence for a short time. It is not to be wondered, if length of time should occasion weariness or sadness; but we must have a strong feeling of attachment when we find it difficult to wait even a single hour. Now, by the <hi type="italic">space of an hour</hi>, he means — a small space of time.<div eID="gen128103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128106" type="x-p"/>This is followed by a correction — that he had been separated from them in <hi type="italic">appearance, not in heart</hi>, that they may know that distance of place does not by any means lessen his attachment. At the same time, this might not less appropriately be applied to the Thessalonians, as meaning that they, on their part, had felt united in <hi type="italic">mind</hi> while absent in <hi type="italic">body;</hi> for it was of no small importance for the point in hand that he should state how fully assured he was of their affection towards him in return. He shews, however, more fully his affection, when he says that he <hi type="italic">endeavored the more abundantly;</hi> for he means that his affection was so far from being diminished by his leaving them, that it had been the more inflamed. When he says, <hi type="italic">we would once and again</hi>, he declares that it was not a sudden heat, that quickly cooled, (as we see sometimes happen,) but that he had been steadfast in this purpose, <note n="552"> <div sID="gen128107" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Hujus propositi tenacem</foreign>. See Hor. Od. 3, 3. 1. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen128107" type="x-p"/> </note> inasmuch as he sought various opportunities.<div eID="gen128106" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128102" osisID="1Thess.2.17" type="section"/>
entries.6069e2e22163ee9d7ed7ae73126311247a910896: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.2.18" sID="gen128108" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18</hi> <hi type="italic"> Satan hindered us</hi>. Luke relates that Paul was in one instance hindered, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.3">Acts 20:3</reference>) inasmuch as the Jews laid an ambush for him in the way. The same thing, or something similar, may have occurred frequently. It is not without good reason, however, that Paul ascribes the whole of this to Satan, for, as he teaches elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.12">Ephesians 6:12</reference>) we have to<div eID="gen128109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128110" type="x-p"/>wrestle not with flesh and blood, but with principalities of the air, and spiritual wickednesses, <hi type="italic">etc.</hi><div eID="gen128110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128111" type="x-p"/>For, whenever the wicked molest us, they fight under Satan’s banner, and are his instruments for harassing us. More especially, when our endeavors are directed to the work of the Lord, it is certain that everything that hinders proceeds from Satan; and would to God that this sentiment were deeply impressed upon the minds of all pious persons — that Satan is continually contriving, by every means, in what way he may hinder or obstruct the edification of the Church! We would assuredly be more careful to resist him; we would take more care to maintain sound doctrine, of which that enemy strives so keenly to deprive us. We would also, whenever the course of the gospel is retarded, know whence the hindrance proceeds. He says elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.13">Romans 1:13</reference>) that God had not permitted him, but both are true: for although Satan does his part, yet God retains supreme authority, so as to open up a way for us, as often as he sees good, against Satan’s will, and in spite of his opposition. Paul accordingly says truly that God does not permit, although the hindrance comes from Satan.<div eID="gen128111" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.2.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128108" osisID="1Thess.2.18" type="section"/>

19 For what is our hope. He confirms that ardor of desire, of which he had made mention, inasmuch as he has his happiness in a manner treasured up in them. “Unless I forget myself, I must necessarily desire your presence, for ye are our glory and joy.” Farther, when he calls them his hope and the crown of his glory, we must not understand this as meaning that he gloried in any one but God alone, but because we are allowed to glory in all God’s favors, in their own place, in such a manner that he is always our object of aim, as I have explained more at large in the first Epistle to the Corinthians.
“Sur la premiere aux Corinth., chap. 1, d. 31;” — “On 1 Corinthians 1:31.”
We must, however, infer from this, that Christ’s ministers will, on the last day, according as they have individually promoted his kingdom, be partakers of glory and triumph. Let them therefore now learn to rejoice and glory in nothing but the prosperous issue of their labors, when they see that the glory of Christ is promoted by their instrumentality. The consequence will be, that they will be actuated by that spirit of affection to the Church with which they ought. The particle also denotes that the Thessalonians were not the only persons in whom Paul triumphed, but that they held a place among many. The causal particle γάρ, (for,) which occurs almost immediately afterwards, is employed here not in its strict sense, by way of affirmation—”assuredly you are.”
CHAPTER 3
1 Thessalonians 3:1-5
1. Wherefore when we could no longer forbear, we thought it good to be left at Athens alone;
1. Quare non amplius sufferentes censuimus, ut Athenis relinqueremur soli:
2. And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith:
2. Et misimus Timotheum fratrem nostrum, et ministrum Dei, et cooperarium nostrum in evangelio Christi, ut confirmaret vos, et vobis animum adderet ex fide nostra,
3. That no man should be moved by these afflictions: for yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto.
3. Ut nemo turbaretur in his afflictionibus: ipsi enim nostis quod in hoc sumus constituti.
4. For verily, when we were with you, we told you before that we should suffer tribulation; even as it came to pass, and ye know.
4. Etenim quum essemus apud vos, praediximus vobis quod essemus afflictiones passuri; quemadmodum etiam accidit, et nostis.
5. For this cause, when I could no longer forbear, I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter have tempted you, and our labour be in vain.
5. Quamobrem et ego non amplius sustinens, misi ut cognoscerem fidem vestram: ne forte tentasset vos, is qui tentat, et exinanitus esset labor noster.

And though God tryeth the hearts of all men, yet especially such as are intrusted with the Gospel. Or these last words may have a more im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediate reference to the foregoing; we speak not as pleasing men, because we know God tryeth our hearts. He vindicates his Ministry from the guilt of three vices which too often attend it; Flattery, Covetousness, and Vain Glory. First, Flattery, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Or, we were not, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> conversant in a word of Flattery, as in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi>; our word was not a word of Flattery, as if we sought to please Men. When we ascribe to men good things that they have not, or above what they have: Or when we applaud or extenuate the evil that is in them, we flatter them: This is reproved often in the false Prophets of the Old Testament, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 30.10. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 13.10, 18. and the false Teachers in the new. The flattery of Ministers is, their preaching of smooth things, ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther to please than profit; when they avoid just reproofs, and searching truths, and close applications, that they may not dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />please, and affect wisdom of words, and rhetorical Discourses, that they may please when they either conceal some part of truth, or pervert it, that people may think their doings better than they are, or their state better than 'tis.</ns0:note>, as ye know <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Their words in preaching being an Overt Act, they themselves could judg of, and therefore the Apostle doth appeal to their own knowledge in that.</ns0:note>; nor a cloak of covetous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.9.</ns0:note> God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> witness <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">In what they could not know, which was their in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward aims and designs, he appeals to God, which is a form of swearing. And in all Oaths men solemnly do concern God therein The same in effect that is call'd protesting, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.31. And that wherein he thus appeals, is, that he had no co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vetous design in his Ministry, which he calls <ns0:hi>a Cloak of Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tousness:</ns0:hi> which lies either in undue withholding what we have, or inordinate desire of more.                <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 5.41, & 12.43.</ns0:note> Nor of men sought we glory <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This is the third vice he vindicates his Ministry from. The word <ns0:hi>Glory</ns0:hi> first signifies some excellency in any Subject. Secondly, This excellency as displaying and manifesting it self. Thirdly, The opinion and esteem thereof in the minds of men, as the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word imports, And so taken in the Text, we did not seek mens honour, high esteem, or applause; we sought them not in the inward bent of our thoughts, or the studies of our mind, nor in the outward course of our Ministry and Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versation, to form them so as to gain Glory from men. Though honour and esteem was their due from men, yet they did not seek it. Honour is to follow men, men not to follow it; This Christ reproved in the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> that in their Prayers, Alms, Fasting, affected Habits, and Titles they sought the praise of men, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6. <ns0:hi>And how can ye believe, seeing ye seek honour one of another, and not the honour that comes from God.</ns0:hi> Joh. 5.44. every man ought with reference to actions honourable, and praise-worthy, and a good Name is a blessing, but to seek honour, that's the evil. And as the Apostle did not seek it himself, so he forbids it to others, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5. <ns0:hi>last. Be not desirous of vain-glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry,</ns0:hi> &c. And notes some false Teachers as guilty of it. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.12. It is a vice directly opposite to humility, unbecoming a man as man, and highly dishonourable to God, and contrary to the Gospel. The Heathens cherisht it as the Spur to great atchievements, It is one of <ns0:hi>Tullies</ns0:hi> Rules for the institution of Princes; but the Christian Religion that gives all Glory to God, condemns it. And yet we may seek the vindication of our Name, when thereby we may provide for the honour of the Name of God, as the Apostle <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> often did.</ns0:note>, neither of you, nor yet of others <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He adds this to shew that this was their general practise among others as well as these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians.</ns0:hi> They were not guilty of flattery, covetous designs, or seeking the Glory of men among any Churches, or in any place. Their practise in their Ministry was uniform, and in all places upright and sincere.</ns0:note>, when we might have been <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 9.3. 2 Thess. 3.9.</ns0:note> burdensome as the apostles of Christ <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Or we were able to be in, or for a burden, Hebraism:</ns0:hi> By burden some understand Authority, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> We might have used our Ministerial Authority more than we did, whereby to get greater honour and respect to our persons among you. And indeed all Authority and Honour have their weight and burden. Others by burden understand maintenance. And then he means we might have been chargeable to you, accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the Power given by Christ to his Apostles to reap car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal things from them to whom they sowed spiritual things. And at the first sending them forth in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> it was so ordained by Christ, that they should be maintained at the peoples charge, see 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. But they were so far from Covetousness, that they took not all that was their due, and what they might of their outward substance,, and from seeking their own honour, that they did not use what Authority they might to procure it among them. For they laboured with their hands night and day, that they might not be chargeable, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 9. Though they might have challenged not only maintenance, but honourable maintenance, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 5.17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 2.3. 2 Cor. 13.4.</ns0:note> we were gentle <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the <ns0:hi>Latin</ns0:hi> takes it for <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> infants, we were as infants to you, as Nurses are as Infants with their Infants, and Children with Children. This is one of the Fruits of the Spirit, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.22. It stands opposite to moroseness, austerity, and rough<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of temper, and is commendable in all, especially Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisters, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.24. And was eminent in Christ, As was prophesied of him, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 40.11. and 42.3. and the contrary he reproveth in <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn, Luk.</ns0:hi> 9.54. It springs from Humility, Meekness, and Patience, as the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />traries, Pride, Passion, and Frowardness. In some cases sharp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and severity may be needful, prudence is to direct therefore our Carriage. The Apostle had now to do with young Converts, and under the Tryal of Persecution, and not Apostates, and obstinate sinners against whom we find he was sometimes severe and sharp, as <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> required, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 22, 23.</ns0:note> among you <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He next gives account of their carriage more positively: And first he speaks of their gentleness among them.</ns0:note>, even as a nurse cherisheth her children <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And he represents this gentleness by that of a Nurse to her Children; not of an hired Nurse, but a Mother Nurse, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 11.12. who useth all tenderness towards them, beareth with their frowardness, condescends to the meanest Offices and em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ployments, and draws out her breasts to them, and lays them in her bosom, and all this to cherish them. And she doth this not out of hope of gain, but out of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>therly affection. Thus saith the Apostle, were we gentle among you. As he conver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted them to Christ, he was their Spiritual Father, but his gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tleness was like that of a Mother, nursing her own Children. He considered their weakness in their first believing, and bore with it; their many Infirmities, Temptations, Afflictions that were upon them, had compassion over them, and supported them under them, and cherisht them with the sincere Milk of Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel Truths; and he did all this not for gain, but out of sincere affection, and willing mind. Some extend the word we ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der <ns0:hi>Nurse</ns0:hi> to the brute Creatures themselves, especially Birds who hatch, and then cherish their young with the warmth of their own body, and care in feeding them; <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the word signifies a feeder, and so may have a more general significati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, see <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 39.14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:515" />8 So being affectionately desirous of you <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">A further account of their behaviour among them. The former verse shewed their great gentleness, this their great love; exprest first in their affectionate desire of them; as the <ns0:hi>Latin</ns0:hi> phrase, <ns0:hi>Cupidissimus sui</ns0:hi> imports, love to the person. And it was the desire of their Salvation, first in their believing, and then perseverance and progress in Faith. It was themselves, and their Goods they desired, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> elsewhere saith, <ns0:hi>We seek not yours, but you.</ns0:hi> Secondly, In the effect of it, which was impart<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Gospel to them; whereby they might be saved; which is amplified by two things. 1. That they did this willingly, not out of meer necessity, with a backward mind; the word is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> we were well-pleased to preach, and with com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />placence of mind. 2. That they were willing to impart their souls to them; that is, to hazard their lives for them in prea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ching to them, as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 16. The same word signifying both the Soul and Life. And he that dies for another, gives his Life to them. Or it may refer to their labours and hardships, whereby they endangered their Lives for them, labouring night and day, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 9. Others understand the words only as an ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression of their great affection to them; a man imparts his Soul to the person whom he entirely loves, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 58.10. when a man gives relief to a person in want out of love, and compassion he imparts his Soul in what he gives. So did they in the Gospel thus preached. And the word <ns0:hi>imparting</ns0:hi> is used to express relief to the wants of the body, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.8. and the Gospel is the bread of Life to give relief to the Soul, and used in this sense also, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.11. The Apostle may here fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther allude to Mothers that are Nurses, who impart not only other food, but their milk, which is their blood to cherish their Children.</ns0:note>, we were willing to have imparted to you not the gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel of God only, but also <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 12.15.</ns0:note> our own souls, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause ye were dear unto us <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or ye have been beloved of us, wherein the Apostle more plainly declares their love to them as the ground of all their labours and perils in preaching to them; yea, it may reach to all that he had said before concerning their carriage among them, all was from love.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 For ye remember brethren <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To make good what he had asserted before about their integrity in preaching the Gospel, that it was without Cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tousness, and vain Glory, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and about their great affection to them therein, he appeals to their own memory.</ns0:note> our labour <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour,</ns0:hi> in what we suffered, attended with care and solicitude of mind; as the word imports:</ns0:note>
                  <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and travel <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">and travel in what we did, attended with weariness, as some distinguish of the words.</ns0:note>: For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 20 34. 1 Cor. 4.12.</ns0:note> labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable to any of you <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This refers to some bodily labour they used, which I find not mentioned in the story while they were at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica,</ns0:hi> though <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> did practice at <ns0:hi>Corinth, Acts</ns0:hi> 18.3. To prevent scandal, and misconstruction that may arise from receiving maintenance, and in case of the Churches poverty the Apostle would refuse it, but without respect to these he pleaded it as his due, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.1, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And his refusing was no work of super-erogation as the Papists plead hence; for in such cases it was a Duty with respect to the honour of his Ministry, so that it ought not to pass into a rule, either that Ministers in no case may labour with their hands to get their bread; or that they ought so to do alwaies, as some would conclude hence, and preach freely: However he commends them that they forgot not the labour and travel they underwent for their sake, and that both night and day, which implies assiduity and diligence as <ns0:hi>Psal</ns0:hi> 1.2. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.37. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 3.10. And so to be taken here. Though it may signifie their spending part of the night as well as the day in some bodily labour; the same we read 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 3.8. yet not to be understood as if they spent the whole night and day therein; for how then could they have preached the Gospel to them as he here addeth; and they would take nothing of maintenance from <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> of them, or be chargeable or burden<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />som to them; not from the poor to whom it might really be a burthen, nor from the rich who yet might be backward, and a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>c<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>unt it a burthen.</ns0:note>, we preached unto you the gospel of God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> witnesses, and God <ns0:hi>also,</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Thess. 3.7.</ns0:note> how ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lily, justly, and unblameably we behaved our selves among you that believe <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The former verse<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> gave account of their carriage in the Ministry, this here of their Christian Conversation, holily, with respect to God, justly, with respect to Duties commanded to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards men, and unblameably, in denying themselves in lawful liberty to avoid all occasion of blame from any of them. And for the truth of this he appeals to themselves; yea, to God himself. There is the witness of men, and the witness of conscience greater than of men, and the witness of God great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est of all, 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.20. He appeals to them witnesses about their external Actions, and to God about the integrity of their hearts: And he doth this not in a way of boasting, but to be an example to them, and as a further reason of the great suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cess of his Ministry. The Conversation of Ministers hath great influence upon the success of their labours.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 As you know how we exhorted and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />forted, and charged every one of you as a father doth his children <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Besides his publick Ministry he dealt more privately with them, as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20.20. And that in a way of exhortation and comfort. By exhortation to quicken them, and by comfort to support them under troubles both outward and inward. And he did this as a Father to his Children, with much earnest<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, Compassion, and Love, yea, and Authority also: He was before represented as a <ns0:hi>Mother, ver.</ns0:hi> 7. And here as a Father whose work and duty is to Exhort, Counsel and Comfort his Children privately at home, so did he as well as publickly, for he was their spiritual Father, as he begat them to Christ by the Gospel, as he tells the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> also, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.15. As before he represented his gentleness, so here his Fatherly care. Or, at their first Conversion he carryed it with gentle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness as a Mother, but afterwards used his Fatherly Authority. And in this he appeals to their own knowledge also, calling their own Consciences to bear witness to what he speaks, that it might leave the greater impression upon them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> unto his kingdom and glory <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Text the word <ns0:hi>charged</ns0:hi> mentioned in the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer verse, begins this verse <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, it signifies testifying, some read it, <ns0:hi>we obtested,</ns0:hi> which is as much as beseeching, others contested, which is a severe charge, containing a threatning, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19.21. <ns0:hi>Charge the people,</ns0:hi> saith God to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> in the Margin, contest the people, or wish the people. It is a charge here which the Apostle gives solemnly in the Name of God to them, calling in the witness of God to it.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Who is calling you</ns0:hi>; Then by Gods Kingdom and Glory we must understand the future state of Heaven: Though they were not yet possest of it, yet by the Gospel God had called them to it, as <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.14. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.10. Or, <ns0:hi>Who hath called you,</ns0:hi> as we read it, then he means their present state since they believed and obeyed the Call of the Gospel, they were brought thereby into Gods Kingdom and Glory. Or, His <ns0:hi>Glorious Kingdom,</ns0:hi> where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in the Glory of God, especially the Glory of his Grace, Mercy, Love, and Wisdom eminently shine forth. Hereupon a Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians Calling is termed an High Calling, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.14. an Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venly Calling, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 3.1. And they being called by God out of Satans Kingdom into this Glorious Kingdom; the Apostle char<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geth them to walk worthy of God and this Calling, by having a Conversation sutable thereunto, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.1. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.10. To walk according to the Laws of this Glorious Kingdom they were already brought into, and suitably to the Glory of Heaven that they were called to the hope of.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>the word of bearing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, ye received it <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 10.4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Gal. 4.14.</ns0:note> not as the word of men <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>ye received not the word of men.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Apostle having given the reasons on his part, and his fellow Ministers, why the Gospel had such effect upon them, he next proceeds to shew the reason on their part, for which he giveth God thanks. And that is from their manner of receiving it. Though this as well as the former are but subordinate rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons. First, they heard it, some will not do that: and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the Apostle here calls it a word of hearing, as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10. an <ns0:hi>Hebraism, Faith cometh by hearing.</ns0:hi> 2. They received it: The word importeth a receiving with affection, as <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> the Virgin <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> to his Wife, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 1.20. 3. They <ns0:hi>received it not as the word of men,</ns0:hi> which we receive sometimes doubting, sometimes disputing it; or believing it only with an humane Faith upon grounds of reason as the dictates of Philosophy, or on the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ports of men; and without the impression of the Authority of God upon our minds, or when we receive the word of God be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of the eloquence or learning of the Preacher, and the affection we bear to him, or admiration of his person, or asthe Papists, we believe it because the Church believeth it.</ns0:note> but (as it is in truth <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>tr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ly.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>) the word of God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">With a Divine Faith, ready Subjection of our souls to it, and with Reverend Attention, as a word that is from Heaven; which the Apostle positively asserts in way of parenthesis. <ns0:hi>As it is in truth,</ns0:hi> or truly, they believed, so he dispersed the word to them, and so they received it. And for this cause he <ns0:hi>gav<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> thanks to God.</ns0:hi> Having mentioned before the subordinate Reasons of the Efficacy of the Word, he now mentions the principal, which is God himself. That any receive the Word as the Word of God, it is not from the Preachers so much as from God. And it is a great cause of Thanksgiving to God, when Ministers find a peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple receive the Word with a Divine Faith, which is not done without Divine Grace: Then they see the fruit of their Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stry, for which they ought to give thanks.</ns0:note>, which effectually worketh al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so in you that believe <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The powerful working of God is usually expressed by this Word, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.19, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2, 13. And the working of Satan also, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.2. men possessed with the Devil, men called <ns0:hi>Energumeni.</ns0:hi> And where the Word is believed and received as the Word of God there it hath this Energy, or worketh effectually, so as to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mote Love, Repentance, Self-denyal, Mortification, Comfort and Peace, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> The Apostle had mentioned before their work of Faith, labour of Love, patience of Hope, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.3. and all from hence, their receiving the Word as the Word of God, and so retaining it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:515" />14 For <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This proves the assertion of the foregoing verse, as the Illative <ns0:hi>For</ns0:hi> doth shew. They were followers of the Churches in <ns0:hi>Iudaea,</ns0:hi> which shewed the word wrought in them effectually. Though the greatest part of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> believed not, yet many did, and hereupon we read of Churches in <ns0:hi>Iudaea.</ns0:hi> Though there was before but one National Church, yet now in Gospel times the Churches were many.</ns0:note> ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God, which in Judea are in Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">And believing in Christ they are called Churches <ns0:hi>in him,</ns0:hi> gathered together in his name, into his institutions, and by his Spirit, and these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> became <ns0:hi>followers,</ns0:hi> or imitators of them, or in the same circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stances with them. The Churches among the Jewes were the first planted, and the Gentile Churches followed them, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />forming to the Faith, Worship and Order that was first in them, yea, and imitating their Faith and Patience in suffering.</ns0:note>; for * ye also have suffered like things of your own countrey-men <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Jewes that believed, suffered from the unbelieving Jewes of their own country, so did these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians.</ns0:hi> But whether the Apostle means only the Gentiles of <ns0:hi>Thessalonica,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> that dwelt there and were born among them, is uncertain. For the persecution mentioned <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 17. was chiefly from the Jewish Synagogue, though the Gentiles might also joyn with them therein.</ns0:note>, even as they <ns0:hi>hav<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:hi> of the Jews <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">They suffered <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> the Churches of <ns0:hi>Iudaea,</ns0:hi> namely, in the same kind, as <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.32, 33, 34. And in the same cause, and with the same joy, constancy and courage: And here Christs words are fulfilled, that a mans Enemies shall be those of his own house, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 10.36.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Who both killed the Lord Jesus <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">No wonder then though they have persecuted you, and the believing <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> their Country-men. They killed the Lord Jesus by the hands of <ns0:hi>Pilate,</ns0:hi> crying, Crucifie him, crucifie him. Though it was by Gods determinate counsel, and the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> power, yet by the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> malice they <ns0:hi>killed him, Mat.</ns0:hi> 21.38. <ns0:hi>This is the heir, let us kill him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and their own prophets, and have <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>sed us <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> persecuted us; and they please not God <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By the figure called Meiosis, its meant they highly displeased God, and were haters of God, and hated, and now rejected of him. Though they had the advantages and reasons to please God above all other people, having had the Law and Ordinan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of his Worship among them, yet they pleased not God. And particularly in their persecutions of the Gospel, and the Apostles though they might think that therein they did God good service, as <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 16.2.</ns0:note>, and are contrary to all men <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Contrary in their worship, laws and customs. Or rather contrary to all men, in hindering the course of the Gospel appointed for mens Salvation. And despising all other Nations in comparison of themselves, they were apt to be Seditious, and raise tumults every where, and to disdain familiarity and common friendship with the <ns0:hi>Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Of their own Nation, and di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rected and sent particularly to them of God; so that it was no new thing in them thus to do. Not that these individual <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> who persecuted <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> killed the Prophets, but they were of the same Nation, the same blood, and of the same spirit with them, and were the children of them that killed the Prophets, as our Saviour charged them, <ns0:hi>Mat</ns0:hi> 23.31. The Spirit of Persecution was natural to them; it descended from one generation to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther: Their Kings were guilty of it, their Priests, their false prophets, and the common people. And though better things might be expected of the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> than any other people, yet thus they did. And it was not only because of the new Doctrine or Worship that the Apostles preached, for they killed their own Prophets before them; but it was their love to their Lusts, ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tred of Reproof, enmity to Holiness, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> that was the cause. And Christ himself chargeth them with the same things, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.37. <ns0:hi>Oh Ierusalem, thou which killest the Prophets, &c.</ns0:hi> And foretells it as that which they would yet practice, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.34.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 13.50. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 14.5, 19. & 18.12 & 19.9.</ns0:note> Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles, that they might be saved <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Their contrariety to all men is exprest particularly in this instance; they forbad the Apostles to preach to the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> which were the greater number of men. Though they opposed also their preaching to the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Nation. For the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> could not endure to hear that the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> should be received into the Church; Or into special favour with God; as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears by Christs Sermon in the Synagogue. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 4.28. And in the Apostles Apology for himself at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem, Acts</ns0:hi> 22.21, 22. And their forbidding them implies, not an Act of Authori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty for they had it not, but their hindring them what they could, and stirring up the people and rulers against them as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 17.6.</ns0:note>, to fill up their sins alway <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">To cause it to rise up to such a measure and degree as will at last bring destruction. Though this was not their intention, yet through the just judgment of God it was the event. They killed the Prophets, but killing Christ and persecut<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Apostles, and hindering the Salvation of Mankind there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by, this fill'd up their sin. The expression alludes to what is said of the <ns0:hi>Amorites, Gen.</ns0:hi> 15.16. and foretold by <ns0:hi>Daniel, chap.</ns0:hi> 9.27. called the consummation; As here is a perfecting of Holiness and filling up of Grace, so also of sin. And sin a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst the Gospel ripens sin more than against the Law. And because they made a constant progress in sin, they are said to fill it up, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.32. <ns0:hi>Fill ye up the measure of your fathers.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">First they filled up their sin, and then comes this wrath, or <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> wrath foretold by <ns0:hi>Daniel, chap.</ns0:hi> 9.27. And by our Saviour <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.38. It was their last destruction by the <ns0:hi>Romans.</ns0:hi> Gods wrath broke forth upon them several times before, but not to the utmost till now; Or, <ns0:hi>to the end,</ns0:hi> as in the <ns0:hi>Greek.</ns0:hi> In former punishments God removed his wrath and restored them again, but this continues to the end. Or some by <ns0:hi>the end,</ns0:hi> un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand only the perfection and consummation of this wrath. And its coming may be read in the <ns0:hi>Greek<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> It hath prevented them</ns0:hi>; as bringing them to judgment before hand in this world. As the destruction of the old World, <ns0:hi>Sodom</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> were figures and forerunners of the last Judgment. And yet this doth not contradict what the Apostle speaks, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11. and many of the Prophets concerning their calling into the Faith and Church of Christ before the end of the World. Also we must understand it with an exception of the remnant of Gods Election that was amongst them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>the time of an hour.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, in presence; not in heart, endeavoured more abundantly to see your face with great desire <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Apostle here makes his Apology, for his so soon de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parting from them, and his continued absence. They were under great sufferings for receiving the Gospel he had preached, and for him therefore to leave them so soon as he did, (as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears in the story, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 16.) and not presently to return, might discourage their hearts and make them question his Love. First for his leaving them, he tells them it was not voluntary but forced by the persecution of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> He being sent away in the night by the brethren to <ns0:hi>Berta. Act.</ns0:hi> 16.10. And therefore he calls it a <ns0:hi>taking away,</ns0:hi> rather then a going away from them. And (as the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word imports) it was secondly a thing grievous to him, as children that are bereft of father and mother, and left Orphans, are greatly troubled. And he was afflicted as a father bereft of children; so were these <ns0:hi>Thes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salonians</ns0:hi> to him having begotten them to Christ by the Gospel. 3. It was but for a short time, <ns0:hi>for the time of an hour,</ns0:hi> when he left them, he intended but a short stay from them, onely to avoid the present storm: Others think he means by the words his sudden leaving them before he took solemn leave of them. 4. He left them in presence, <ns0:hi>quoad faciem,</ns0:hi> as to outward sight not in heart. The proper genius of true Lovers, who are pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent with each other in soul when separated in body, 5. He tells them of his endeavours to see their face; and that the more abundantly because he came away so suddenly from them. And Lastly, He did this with great desire, his endeavours here<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in were acted with great Affection.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Wherefore we would have come unto you, (even I Paul <ns0:hi>z</ns0:hi>) once and again, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.13. & 15.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tan hindred us <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either by raising up disputes against the Gospel at <ns0:hi>Athens</ns0:hi> by the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />losophers there, which he was concerned to stay and answer, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 15. Or else by stirring up wicked men to lye in wait for him in the way: Or by raising Tumults as the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> did at <ns0:hi>Berea,</ns0:hi> whereby he was constrained <ns0:hi>to go as it were to the Sea, Act.</ns0:hi> 16.14. Or by sowing dissensions in other Chur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches which detained him to end them. Or by what way it was, is somewhat uncertain. But being thus hindred it made his desire the more fervent by the opposition.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And hereby we see Satans Enmity to the Gospel, especially to Churches new planted, that they might nor take rooting.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">This he adds further to satisfie them of his real affection to them, that he attempted to come to them once and again, that is often, as <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 13.20. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.16. and that they might be assured it was not his Fellow Ministers desire onely to come. Therefore he expresseth his own name particularly in a Paren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thesis (even I <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>) Or by his saying, <ns0:hi>even I Paul,</ns0:hi> he assures them concerning his own desire to come to them; At least I <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> though others did not so; as the <ns0:hi>French</ns0:hi> Bible reads it. And he had come to them had not Satan hindred him.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:517" />19 For * what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> our hope <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Here the Apostle gives the reason of his desire to see them. He first calls them his hope; that is, the matter of his hope, that among others they should be saved in the day of Christ.</ns0:note>, or joy <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Secondly, <ns0:hi>His joy</ns0:hi>: He at present rejoyced in their ready and sincere receiving the Gospel preached by him.</ns0:note>, or crown of ‖ rejoycing <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thirdly, <ns0:hi>His crown of rejoycing,</ns0:hi> which signifies the triumph and height of joy; and seeing he mentions the presence and coming of Jesus Christ, he looks to the Crown that he should receive at that day, which he speaks of 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.25. And these <ns0:hi>Thes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salonians</ns0:hi> among others would help to make up this crown of rejoycing to him. And in the words we may observe an emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent gradation, as also that the Crown of Ministers will arise not onely from Christ, but from their people also.</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> not even ye in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For ye are our glory and joy <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He redoubles the expression to shew his great affection, and complacency of hearts in them. Or to shew that they more than others were this occasion of rejoycing to him. And he mentions <ns0:hi>glory</ns0:hi> as well as <ns0:hi>joy,</ns0:hi> for the great success of his Ministry among them, would redound to his glory in the day of Christ, as <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 12.3. <ns0:hi>They that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever and ever.</ns0:hi> Or they were his glory at present, a glory to his Ministry, and a Seal to his Apostleship.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
